title: Why Do the Wicked Live On? Job Answers the Friends
summary: Job asks his friends to listen, then flatly contradicts their teaching. The wicked often live long, prosper, raise happy children, and die in peace, even while telling God to leave them alone. Punishment deferred to their children is no justice, and death levels the prosperous and the bitter alike. The friends' comfort, Job concludes, is empty and false.
story: This chapter closes the second cycle of speeches. Eliphaz (chapter 15), Bildad (chapter 18), and Zophar (chapter 20) have each painted the downfall of the wicked, and each portrait was aimed at Job. Until now Job has mostly spoken about his own suffering and his relationship with God. Here, for the first time, he takes on the friends' doctrine as a claim about the world and tests it against the evidence. It is his most direct rebuttal in the book. The friends will not change their position in response. In the third cycle Eliphaz will go further still and accuse Job of specific crimes (chapter 22), while Job turns back to his longing to find God (chapter 23).
historical:
The chapter reflects the same undated, patriarchal setting in Uz as the rest of the dialogue, but its argument appeals to something every ancient reader could check: common experience. Job points to travelers (verse 29), those who move along the trade routes of the Near East and bring back reports from many lands. Their testimony, he says, is that the evil man is often spared in the day of calamity and buried with honor.

Job is not the only ancient voice to notice this. Israel's own Scriptures raise the same observation: Psalm 73 describes the prosperity of the arrogant, Jeremiah asks why the way of the wicked prospers (Jeremiah 12:1), and Ecclesiastes observes righteous people who perish and wicked people who live long. Mesopotamian wisdom texts also contain laments of a righteous sufferer who cannot understand why the gods treat him as they do. Job gives the question its sharpest form.
cultural:
Job's picture of the prosperous wicked is a picture of everything an ancient household hoped for: children growing up around them, homes safe from fear, bulls that breed and cows that calve without miscarriage, and children dancing to the tambourine, lyre, and flute (verses 8-12). These were real instruments of the time; the lyre (kinnor) was a small stringed instrument, the tambourine a hand drum, and the pipe a wind instrument. To go down to Sheol in peace (verse 13) was the ideal death, quick and untroubled at the end of a full life. Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, the shadowy place to which all the dead were thought to go.

The lamp of the wicked (verse 17) picks up Bildad's image in 18:5-6: in a house, a lamp burning through the night was a sign of life and prosperity, and a lamp put out meant the household had ended. Verse 19 quotes a common belief that God stores up a man's punishment for his children. Job rejects it as unjust. The burial scene at the end (verses 32-33) reflects the honor of a great man's funeral, a crowd following the bier and a watch kept over the tomb.
literary: The chapter is a disputation speech, an argument that quotes the opponents' positions and answers them. Job begins with a plea for a hearing (verses 1-6) and then states his thesis as a question: “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” (verse 7). He develops it with a portrait of prosperity (verses 8-16) that deliberately mirrors the friends' portraits of ruin, answering Zophar's picture in chapter 20 almost point for point. Then come a series of rhetorical questions, How often? (verses 17-18), and quotations of the friends' own sayings (verses 19 and 28), each followed by Job's rebuttal. A short reflection on death as the great leveler (verses 23-26) sets two men side by side, one full of vigor, one bitter, both covered by worms. The final verse returns to the opening word: the friends were asked for consolation (verse 2), and they have offered empty words (verse 34).

outline.t: The wicked prosper and tell God to leave them alone
How often is the lamp of the wicked put out?
Death comes to the prosperous and the bitter alike
The friends' arguments answered and dismissed

doctrines.note: Job insists that God's government of the world cannot be read off the fortunes of individuals. The prosperity of the wicked is real, and Job refuses to deny it for the sake of a tidy theology. Scripture's teaching on providence must make room for what Job sees.

Job does not deny that God judges; he asks why judgment is so often absent in this life. The question pushes beyond this world toward a reckoning the friends never consider, a theme the Old Testament develops slowly and the New Testament states openly.
If the wicked often prosper, then the righteous often suffer, and suffering cannot be treated as proof of guilt. That conclusion is the ground on which Job stands throughout the book.

words.note: Rasha, wicked or guilty. It is the standard term for the person in the wrong, both morally and in a legal case. It appears four times in this chapter, beginning with Job's question in verse 7. Job borrows the friends' favorite subject and turns their own word against their conclusions.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. In most of the Old Testament it is simply the place all the dead go, good and bad alike, and not a place of punishment. Job's point in verse 13 is that the wicked reach it peacefully, with no sign that anything distinguishes their end.

Tanchum, consolation or comfort. Job asks that the friends' listening be his consolation (verse 2). The friends came to comfort him (2:11), and the related verb appears in verse 34, where Job asks how they can comfort him with empty words. The chapter is framed by the comfort they failed to give.

Hevel, vapor, breath, or emptiness. It is the key word of Ecclesiastes, often translated vanity or meaningless. Here it describes the friends' words in verse 34: they have no more substance than a breath.

christ: Job's complaint that justice is missing from this life finds its answer in the New Testament only by way of a greater story. Jesus himself acknowledged that God sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45) and told the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), in which a man who lived in luxury and a poor man who suffered find their places reversed after death. The New Testament locates final justice in the judgment that follows the resurrection, and it grounds that hope in the resurrection of Jesus, the righteous one who suffered and was vindicated by God. This does not appear in Job 21 as prophecy. The link is that Job asks a question this life cannot answer, and the gospel answers it beyond this life without pretending, as the friends did, that the question isn't real.

hard.q: Is Job right that the wicked prosper and God does nothing?
hard.a: Job's observation is true to experience and is confirmed elsewhere in Scripture, which is why the book lets it stand. Psalm 73, Jeremiah 12, and Ecclesiastes all describe the same thing. The friends' position, that the wicked are always visibly punished in this life, is the one the book rejects (42:7). At the same time, Job speaks in anguish and in the extremity of his argument; he does not claim that God never judges, only that the pattern the friends describe does not hold. Interpreters answer his challenge in several ways. Some stress that the Old Testament gradually points toward judgment and life beyond death (Daniel 12:2 is the clearest example), which changes the terms of the question. Others emphasize that the book of Job does not give a theoretical answer at all: God's speeches in chapters 38 to 41 call Job to trust a wisdom larger than any formula. Most Christian readers hold both. The prosperity of the wicked is real, final justice is still ahead, and in the meantime faith must live without a visible scoreboard.

questions: Job asks his friends simply to listen. Why is listening so hard when someone we care about is making an argument we find threatening?
Where have you seen people who reject God living long and comfortable lives? How does that affect your faith?
Job refuses to accept that God punishes children for their parents' sins (verses 19-21). What does his objection show about his sense of justice, and where did he learn it?
